entries.title: Minority Collective Action for User-Side Fairness
entries.venue: ACM Conference on Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization (EAAMO)
entries.abstract: Machine learning models often preserve biases present in training data, leading to unfair treatment of certain minority groups. Despite an array of existing firm-side bias-mitigation techniques, these methods typically incur utility costs and require organizational buy-in. Recognizing that many models rely on user-contributed data, end-users can induce fairness through the framework of Algorithmic Collective Action. In this setting, a coordinated minority group strategically relabels its own data to enhance fairness without altering the firm’s training process. We design practical, model-agnostic, minority-only collective-action methods and validate them on real-world datasets. Our findings show that a subgroup of the minority can substantially reduce unfairness with little impact on overall prediction error.

entries.title: Fairness in infectious disease modeling
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT The concept of fairness has been extensively examined within the domains of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence more broadly. It remains, however, largely underexplored in the field of Computational Epidemiology. Considering the substantial influence that epidemic models exert on public health policy, particularly in the context of outbreak preparedness and response, this shortcoming is of great relevance. Here, we propose a mathematical framework, grounded in core principles from Social Epidemiology, for evaluating the fairness of computational epidemic models. We begin by applying our framework to a range of epidemic modeling approaches and simulation scenarios, such as the initial spread of COVID-19 in London, New York, and Santiago de Chile, as well as the 2016 Zika virus outbreak in Colombia, demonstrating its consistent capacity to assess model fairness across diverse disease dynamics. Subsequently, we illustrate how our definition of fairness can be incorporated into the design of immunization strategies as a way to enhance health equity while simultaneously improving the overall effectiveness of such interventions. Overall, our results offer a new systematic methodology for quantifying fairness in computational epidemiology.

entries.title: FairSEP: Harmonizing Multiple Fairness Metrics in Graph Neural Networks via Pareto Optimization
entries.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
entries.abstract: Group fairness in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) aims to mitigate performance disparities across demographic groups. While existing methods primarily focus on Demographic Parity and Equal Opportunity, Predictive Equality (ΔFPR) remains under-explored, potentially leading to disparate error risks. Furthermore, these methods often rely on a single surrogate loss of fairness, which is insufficient to achieve multiple fairness criteria simultaneously. Moreover, these methods often apply uniform debiasing across different label groups, making it difficult to separately address group disparities in the positive and negative classes. Consequently, achieving an optimal trade-off between utility and multiple fairness metrics remains challenging. To address these issues, we propose FairSEP, a unified Pareto-optimized framework. Specifically, we construct a sensitive subspace from per-class centroid differences between sensitive groups, debias embeddings by removing their subspace projections, and enforce prediction consistency between original and debiased representations. On this basis, we introduce a conditional Wasserstein loss that minimizes the Wasserstein distance between predictive distributions of sensitive groups conditioned on true labels, explicitly reducing disparate error rates across groups. Finally, we design a Pareto-based strategy that automatically adjusts the loss weights to resolve conflicts between different objectives. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that FairSEP achieves a superior trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
